query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that separately computes the lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr—by explicitly modeling atomic-scale lattice distortions with machine-learned force fields (via Green–Kubo formalism) for phonon transport and calculating electron scattering using DFT-derived Boltzmann transport—will more accurately reproduce the independent temperature trends of each contribution. Specifically, it will predict a lattice thermal conductivity that is approximately 20–30% lower (i.e., closer to experimental totals) than earlier Debye temperature‐based models above 300 K, while also capturing the near parity of lattice and electronic conductivities observed below 200 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy (with variants having controlled low-level oxygen impurities, e.g., approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, as used in experiments).
generation.intervention: Apply a multiscale simulation framework that decouples heat transport by (a) computing lattice thermal conductivity using on‐the‐fly machine‐learned force fields and Green–Kubo methods to capture atomic-scale static and dynamic distortions, and (b) evaluating electronic thermal conductivity through DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations.
generation.conditions: Measurements should be performed over two temperature regimes: below 200 K to resolve the near-equal contributions of lattice and electronic heat transport, and from 300 K to 1200 K (using samples with controlled oxygen levels) to compare total thermal conductivity against experimental values (10–17 W/(K m)).
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from atomic-size mismatches and non-ideal positional deviations within the disordered crystal lattice.
generation.mechanism: By directly accounting for the static and dynamic distortions in the lattice (which modulate phonon scattering) and independently evaluating electron-scattering processes, the model avoids the conflation inherent in average Debye-temperature or perfect crystal approximations, thereby reducing systematic errors and better predicting the overall and component thermal transport properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Above 300 K, the lattice thermal conductivity predicted by the new approach should be lower by roughly 20–30% than that given by previous models, aligning with the low total conductivity measured experimentally (especially when 1 wt.% oxygen is present). Below 200 K, the approach will indicate that lattice and electronic thermal conductivities are of comparable magnitude.
generation.baseline: Earlier predictive methods based on Debye temperature estimates and defect-free, averaged perfect-crystal models, which tend to either conflate or misestimate the lattice and electronic contributions and feature larger uncertainties (up to ±30% error).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to high-entropy alloys with significant chemical disorder and well-characterized microstructures; deviations may occur in alloys with additional phases, high defect densities, or stronger electron–phonon interactions beyond the model’s current treatment.
generation.uncertainty: The estimated 20–30% improvement in predictive accuracy is based on literature comparisons and simulation trends; however, the exact quantitative improvement remains uncertain until validated by experimental decoupling of the thermal contributions. The effect of oxygen impurity levels and possible microstructural variations also introduces uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples, including a set with a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen level. Perform temperature-dependent thermal measurements from well below 200 K to 1200 K. Use separate techniques, such as time-domain thermoreflectance or transient grating methods for the lattice contribution and electrical conductivity measurements (combined with Wiedemann–Franz law evaluation) for the electronic contribution.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity as a function of temperature
Electronic thermal conductivity as a function of temperature
Total thermal conductivity across the 50 K to 1200 K range
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for temperatures above 300 K, the lattice thermal conductivity deviates by more than ±10% from the model’s predictions or if below 200 K the separate contributions do not appear to be comparable, then the hypothesis is falsified. Similarly, if the total conductivity measured in oxygen-doped samples falls outside the range of 10–17 W/(K m) predicted by the decoupled model, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution. Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging.
